P1.evidence: No opening and no frame of any kind. There was no setter, so P1a's conditional does not apply. The prospect simply began — 'just a little bit of background on myself' — and self-narrated for four minutes before the rep's first question, which was a detail probe ('Can I stop you for a second? When you do the strength training five to six times a week, what kind of strength training?'). The four-part frame was never set, no agreement was sought, and the scripted open question was never asked because the prospect got there first. It cost little on this call because the prospect was forthcoming, but it is the reason the price conversation arrived cold at the 57-minute mark with no expectation that a decision was due today.

P2.evidence: Five hits, and the nutrition work is the most thorough in the batch — a full day walkthrough, cheat frequency and its time of day, soda, alcohol, eating-out frequency and cuisine, and cooking oils. Work asked and pursued into the dual US-and-Asia hours and their stress. Injuries asked explicitly and followed up: 'with this lower back sciatica, is there anything apart from that, that it's limiting your movements? You mentioned the shoulder, but is there anything else?' Training week interrogated down to the split. Results from current training asked twice and well — 'How long have you been stuck at this weight currently that you're at?' and 'how do you feel after those classes? Is anything popping up, flaring up?' Age, height and weight all arrived unprompted, so P2a is partial despite the data existing. Health conditions were never asked as a general question — no medications, no bloodwork — which matters for a 56-year-old. Sleep was never asked at all, despite the prospect volunteering night-time leg cramping, and energy was inferred rather than asked, though the rep's read on the afternoon willpower-depletion pattern was genuinely good.

P3.evidence: The only goals phase in this batch that actually reached the deep why, and it is a model for the rest. The big-why question ran — 'what would be your, like, big why behind this? Like, why do you want to do this?' — and then the bridge landed properly: 'when you think about it, in six months, right, when you finally weigh 170, you look in the mirror, who do you see?' answered 'I feel like more confidence.' Rather than accepting that, the rep drove one level further with 'confidence is a big one. When you think about it, like what this extra confidence would give you that you're not maybe going for right now?', which produced the real material — feeling stuck and bogged down by work, wanting a better handle on his life, and unprompted, 'maybe I could have a better relationship with my wife and my son.' The rep then reused it correctly at the hard moment ('when it's going to suck, and you're going to think about why are you doing this... you think about your family, you think about your son') and again at the price, tying the number to the why: 'to get you to that, your goals to be 170, be confident, show up for your family, the full investment for that is 6K.' The who-else question was never asked outright — the prospect volunteered family — and the can't-do material came from his own Spain and Hawaii stories rather than from the question.

P4.evidence: Past attempts and outcomes surfaced through the prospect's flare-up narrative rather than through questions — chiropractor, stretches, hyperextensions, yoga, the gym split, cardio classes. The 'why didn't it stick' question was never asked. But the gap got named cleanly by the prospect twice: 'this journey has always, it's just really been on my own and just be just trying to, I feel like, I just need some guidance' and 'over the years I've tried to do it on my own but failed.' The rep then ran a strong functional equivalent of P4f rather than the scripted line: 'the best athletes in the world need coaches, and they have like multiple ones. So why we, like regular people, tend to think that, oh, I don't need a coach. Are you saying that you're better than LeBron James and Kobe Bryant?' It produced the concession the phase exists for — 'Yeah, I'm not smart enough, man. I came to that conclusion. I need guidance. Let me try it. Let me try the coaching.'

P5.evidence: The nearest any call in this batch has come, and still a miss. The rep delivered a consequence frame as a warning rather than a question: 'as you get older, that's why it's so common that elder people, when they fall on the ground, they break their hip. And usually what it means, they end up dying afterwards.' That is a two-year projection told at the prospect, and it does the job of P5a in the wrong direction — the script wants the prospect to describe his own future, not to be handed a mortality scenario. The rep noticed himself and pulled back: 'let's not talk about morbid pictures.' None of P5b, P5c or P5d ran. The material for a proper consequence frame was sitting right there — a flare cycle every four to five months, a cane in Barcelona, a hotel room in Hawaii — and asking 'what does the next two years look like if that cycle continues?' would have been both stronger and cleaner than the falling-and-dying passage.

P6.evidence: The only complete commitment check in the batch. The belief question ran twice — 'Do you feel like this approach would actually work for you?' and 'How do you feel about it? Like, does it check all the boxes for you?', answered 'It does. It does.' The all-in question then ran in near-scripted form and with the identity hook attached: 'if we can figure out all the logistical details, are you fully committed to showing up and doing the work to become that new version of Patrick?' The answer was unambiguous and specific — 'Yeah, yeah. I feel like I'm at that point where I already have a schedule. I already have that commitment... I already have time blocked off already.' A clear yes was banked before any price was mentioned, which is precisely why the price objections that followed were handled from strength rather than by discounting.

P11.evidence: Payment collected in full and confirmed live — 'i see it went through' — for $6,000, the only full-price cash close in this batch. Onboarding with Trevor booked for August 17 at 12:15pm Pacific from five offered slots, correctly scheduled around the prospect's return from Europe. The agreement email arrived and was opened on the call ('I have the coaching agreement open'), but the signature confirmation at 01:10:31 is garbled and cannot be treated as complete, so P11c is partial. Step four is partial too: Primal University was mentioned but explicitly deprioritised — 'you can sign up in your own time... No hurry with that at all' — and no onboarding questionnaire was mentioned at all, even though other calls in this batch describe one as required before the Trevor session.

objection_plays.detail: Three separate price probes: 'Is that the cheapest?', 'I need a little bit lower amount if it's not working with Trevor', and 'Is $6,000 the best price with Trevor?' The rep handled the last two well. He held the price outright — 'we don't have, like, discounts' — which is the correct answer and the opposite of what he did on the Chris Wiley and Bennu calls. He isolated properly: 'let's zoom out. Like, talk to me. What's up with the price?' and diagnosed correctly with 'is it that you don't have the full amount right now, or is it more of the structure of the payment?' He then ran an effective takeaway — 'I don't want to put you in a financial difficult situation... if it's not possible, or that would mean that you're going to have to stretch yourself extremely' — and the prospect immediately committed: 'No, it's fine. Let's go with it.' What did not run was the financial picture: no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no cards, no available credit, no investments. And the first probe was mishandled in a way the script does not cover — he disclosed that a cheaper coach tier exists and then declined to price it.

Two triggers. The specific one was injury fear — 'I'm worried about doing it correctly. just seems, you know, that I might hurt' and later 'I'm just really concerned about form, getting the right form' — answered with the first-month technique focus and the video feedback loop rather than with any OE move. The general one was a stated risk aversion — 'I've always been the safe guy, the safe route' — and here the rep did run a real bridge: 'all the best things in the are on the other side of fear. And you in your business probably had to make difficult, uncomfortable decisions many times... If you would stay comfortable, you wouldn't be in your position as you are right now.' That is well-targeted at a finance professional and it landed. The certainty question, the plane, and the burned-before moves did not run.

Trigger was a three-week European holiday starting at the end of the week. The rep attempted the right reframe first — hotel gyms usually have kettlebells, so the schedule can absorb it, and the prospect agreed to check — but then accepted a start date three and a half weeks out without running any of the never-slows-down moves. Defensible here: the deal was already closed at full price and the delay is a genuine fixed obstacle rather than an excuse, so pushing would have risked the close for little gain. Scored partial rather than miss because the travel-start reframe is the substance of the play even though the scripted lines did not run.

SCRIPT GAP, and the most serious clinical instance in this batch. The prospect disclosed a recurring lumbar sciatica cycle that disables him for a month every four to five months, with the most recent episode two months earlier, plus cervical symptoms radiating down the left arm to the elbow, plus heel and Achilles pain, managed only by a chiropractor. He then raised his own injury fear unprompted. The playbook has no clearance gate, so the rep answered a clinical disclosure with a training claim — that the heel pain and the back flares are strength deficits — and prescribed overhead halos. No physician assessment was suggested at any point. Note the perverse incentive this creates: the same condition was then used as the reason he must take the more expensive tier.

SCRIPT GAP — the undisclosed tier. Asked 'Is that the cheapest?', the rep revealed that coaching with one of Trevor's coaches is available at a lower price and then refused to quote it, steering up on clinical grounds. The prospect explicitly asked for the number ('I need a little bit lower amount if it's not working with Trevor') and never received it. There is no guidance in the playbook on when the junior-coach tier should be offered, what it costs, or how to present the choice, so the rep improvised a steer. The principal needs to decide whether that tier is a real product; if it is, withholding its price from a prospect who directly asked is a problem.

notes: The best-executed call in this batch and the template the others should be scored against: P3 reached the real why and the rep reused it at the close, P6 ran completely, the price was held against three separate probes without a discount, and the result was the only full-price cash close in the batch. Two things to fix, neither of which was needed to win the deal. First, when a buyer asks whether a cheaper tier exists and the answer is yes, quote it. Second and far more important, this rep is now three calls into a pattern of answering disclosed clinical conditions with training assertions and his own avoided-surgery anecdote; a mandatory clearance gate in P2d would have cost this sale nothing and is overdue.
